strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: predicting transcriptional responses to genetic perturbations, especially for unseen and combinatorial perturbations.
The proposed scBIG framework is conceptually clear, combining module induction, structured encoding, flow matching, and structure-aware alignment in a coherent pipeline.
The empirical evaluation is extensive, covering two widely used benchmarks (Norman and Replogle2022_rpe1), 13 baselines, multiple metrics, and several perturbation settings.
Ablation studies support the contributions of the main components: Gene-Relation Clustering, Gene-Cluster-Aware Encoder, and the two biological consistency losses.
The biological analyses (pathway enrichment of gene clusters and attention-shift case studies) provide useful interpretability and support the biological plausibility of the induced modules.
The limitations discussion in Appendix A.6 honestly acknowledges static module structure, dependence on external priors, and limited zero-shot generalization scope.
weaknesses: Potential data leakage: Section A.3.1 describes encoder-decoder pretraining on an expression matrix X ∈ R^{N×G} without stating whether validation/test cells are excluded. If pretraining uses all cells, including those with held-out perturbations, the holdout results are invalid because the encoder would have seen test perturbation responses.

The cluster correlation alignment loss is ill-defined as written. Eq. (7) and Algorithm 3 (lines 20–21) describe computing a K×K Pearson correlation matrix from a single cell’s K-dimensional cluster-aggregated vector, which is mathematically impossible. The manuscript does not clarify whether this is a batch-level statistic, how batches with multiple perturbations are handled, or how the target R*_gt is computed and aligned per cell.

The method for encoding combinatorial (double-gene) perturbations is not described, despite being central to the Norman additive split. It is unclear how ESM2 embeddings of two perturbed genes are combined (e.g., sum, concatenation, averaging) to form the condition vector c for dual perturbations.

The pathway-informed optimal transport loss lacks essential implementation details: the cost matrix, normalization of pathway activation vectors, Sinkhorn regularization, and how S_gt* is computed per perturbation. This makes the objective difficult to reproduce and assess.

Reproducibility gaps remain despite the code statement: GRC’s Sinkhorn parameters and capacity-constrained rounding algorithm are not specified; the pathway OT details are omitted; and the main tables lack error bars for most baselines, with standard deviations reported only for a subset in Appendix A.2.

Presentation quality is weak: numerous typos and inconsistencies (e.g., “Unlasting,” “CellFlow,” metric names such as ρΔ0/ρΔU, ACCΔ0/ACCΔU, inconsistent table headers), and many references have incorrect years (e.g., Aibar et al. 2023 vs. 2017; Norman et al. 2022 vs. 2019; Wolf et al. 2022 vs. 2018). These errors reduce confidence in the manuscript’s rigor.

Baseline fairness is not fully established. Some baselines are adapted in non-standard ways (e.g., CellFlow using 50-dimensional PCA, foundation models fine-tuned for 20 epochs), and it is unclear whether all methods received comparable hyperparameter tuning or condition-encoding capabilities.

The claimed “average improvement of 6.7% over strongest baselines” is not clearly defined or computed, and the main tables report no confidence intervals, making it hard to judge the statistical significance of the reported gains.

strengths: The problem is well-motivated: perturbation responses are genuinely coordinated and program-level, and the critique of flat gene-wise representations and static biological graphs is reasonable.

The experimental effort is substantial: 13 baselines across four paradigms, two benchmarks (Norman additive/holdout, Replogle RPE1), plus ablations, 5-seed robustness, and efficiency analysis (Tables 1-4, 5-8).
The GRC ablation (Table 4a) does provide some evidence that module-level clustering contributes: GRC+Normal reaches 0.8348 ρΔ vs. 0.7781 for the unordered baseline, and GRC+GCAE reaches 0.8496.
Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: code is provided, hyperparameters are tabulated (Table 9), and full algorithmic pseudocode is given (Algorithms 1-3).
The pathway enrichment (Fig. 3, 8, 9) and attention-shift analyses (Fig. 4) make a genuine attempt at biological interpretability rather than pure black-box reporting.
The limitations section (A.6) honestly discusses static priors, module granularity, and the narrow evaluation scope.
weaknesses: The central claim that a *module-level inductive bias* drives the gains is not cleanly isolated. From Table 4a, GRC alone accounts for most of the improvement (0.8348 vs. 0.7781), while the GCAE adds only ~1.5% (0.8496). The 'module' framing is therefore oversold relative to the marginal contribution of the proposed structured encoder.

Potential target leakage: L_corr and L_pathway are supervised against ground-truth perturbation statistics R*gt(p) and S*gt(p) that are cached per condition (Algorithms 3, §2.4). The mechanism by which these regularizers transfer to truly unseen perturbations is never explained, and part of the reported gains may stem from condition-specific target statistics rather than a generalizable module inductive bias.

Novelty is incremental. Every component — Perceiver-style latent bottleneck (Jaegle et al., 2021), conditional flow matching, Sinkhorn/OT clustering, cluster correlation alignment, pathway OT — is an existing technique; the contribution is a recombination applied to perturbation prediction.

The results partly contradict the narrative. Linear-scGPT achieves competitive error metrics on the holdout double-gene task (MSE 3.91 vs. scBIG 3.68; MAE 0.0626 vs. 0.0554), and on RPE1 several baselines are within ~0.01-0.02 on ρΔ/ACC, so the claimed advantages are narrower than presented.

Presentation and correctness issues: Table 2 reports 'ACCΔ0' where 'ACCΔD' is intended; the DES definition in Eq. 14 places ŷ_ctrl,sig in both numerator and denominator (a typo); the abstract's '6.7% average improvement' is not traceable to any stated aggregation; and Table 5 reports a *negative* per-step overhead for L_corr that the authors dismiss as 'measurement noise,' which is unconvincing.

The interpretability analysis (Fig. 4) rests on two hand-selected case studies (NOL8, KCTD10), which is too thin to support the strong claim that scBIG 'captures the underlying biological mechanisms of gene regulation.'
The 'adaptive' module induction is largely static: GRC is solved once offline and clusters are fixed (§2.1), which partially undercuts the paper's criticism that prior work relies on static priors.

Evaluation-protocol questions: the PDS metric and Control baseline (fixed at 0.5000) are idiosyncratic, and the RPE1 evaluation covers only single-gene perturbations, so combinatorial generalization is not actually tested on that dataset.

strengths: Addresses an important problem in perturbation prediction by introducing a module-level inductive bias, motivated by coordinated program-level transcriptional responses.
Integrates multiple biological priors (foundation-model gene embeddings, high-confidence PPI, Reactome pathway memberships, ESM2 perturbation embeddings) into a unified framework.

Extensive empirical evaluation on two benchmarks (Norman, Replogle RPE1) across additive, holdout, unseen single/double perturbation settings, with 13 baselines, ablations, robustness, efficiency, and biological analyses.

Reports strong and consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, especially on out-of-distribution and combinatorial settings (e.g., +38.0% on ρΔD for unseen single perturbations, +34.9% on ρΔD for RPE1).
Good reproducibility practices: code in supplementary, detailed hyperparameters, algorithm pseudocode, dataset splits, and an honest limitations section.
weaknesses: The core claim of module-inductive generative modeling is weakened because the GCAE compresses all module representations into a single global latent vector Z (mean over modules) and the conditional flow matching operates only on this global vector. Inter-program interactions are not explicitly maintained in the generative process; structure-aware losses are auxiliary and operate on decoded expression rather than latent module dynamics.

No internal ablation isolates the benefit of module-level modeling from the rest of the architecture: the 'Normal' encoding ablation is ambiguous (does it operate on gene-wise or cluster-wise input?), and there is no comparison to a gene-wise model with the same flow-matching backbone. Thus the source of gains is not fully established.

The Pathway-informed Optimal Transport loss is technically questionable: it computes Sinkhorn distance between two pathway-activation vectors (S x̂1 and S x1) with uniform weights over pathways. This is permutation-invariant and does not enforce pathway-specific identity; it effectively compares sorted pathway activation distributions rather than aligning each pathway to its correct target. A direct MSE or identity-constrained OT would be more appropriate.

GRC enforces strictly balanced clusters (|c_k| = G/K), which is biologically arbitrary and may split large pathways or merge unrelated genes. The justification is computational (equal attention capacity) rather than biological, and the ablation only compares against unbalanced K-means on these two datasets.
Some baselines may be disadvantaged: CellOracle's n_iters was reduced from 100,000 to 1,000, which likely harms its performance, and other baselines trained from scratch may not be optimally tuned.

Overclaims relative to the method: the introduction promises 'context-adaptive' and 'dynamic program reorganization,' but GRC induces a single, static, offline partition per dataset using fixed PPI and foundation-model embeddings; it does not adapt module structure to different cell types or perturbation conditions.

Missing reproducibility details: exact Sinkhorn regularization ε, capacity-constrained rounding procedure, number of GRC alternating iterations T, pairing strategy for control/perturbed cells in flow matching, ODE solver settings, and decoder architecture are not fully specified.

Presentation issues: notation is confusing (x1 used for both ground-truth and predicted expression), Algorithm 3 line 18 has a typo (x1 ← Dψ(zt) should likely be x̂1 ← Dψ(z1)), and several tables/figures are small or have formatting inconsistencies.

Statistical significance is not established in the main results: tables lack error bars/confidence intervals; only Norman standard deviations across five seeds are provided in the appendix, with no variance reported for RPE1. The biological attention-shift analysis is anecdotal (two perturbations, no statistical test).

strengths: Addresses an important problem in functional genomics: predicting transcriptional responses to genetic perturbations, with emphasis on combinatorial and out-of-distribution generalization.
Proposes a well-motivated module-level inductive bias that explicitly models coordinated gene programs, moving beyond gene-wise representations.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (Norman, RPE1, ComboSciPlex), multiple splits (additive, holdout, cross-cell-line transfer), and 13 baselines.
Ablation studies demonstrate the contribution of each component (GRC, GCAE, biological alignment losses) and include hyperparameter sensitivity and efficiency analyses.

Biological validation through pathway enrichment of induced clusters, perturbation-specific cross-module coordination, and attention shift case studies provides interpretability and supports biological plausibility.
Strong reproducibility: code provided, detailed hyperparameters, public datasets, clear algorithmic descriptions, and model checkpoints promised.
Statistical rigor: standard deviations across seeds, confidence intervals, and paired Wilcoxon tests against the strongest baseline.
Honest and thorough limitations discussion covering zero-shot generalization scope, static module induction, and dependence on external priors.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method combines existing techniques (optimal transport clustering, Perceiver-style bottleneck, conditional flow matching, correlation alignment, pathway optimal transport) with modest modifications; the core idea of using gene modules or pathways for perturbation prediction is not entirely new.

GRC clustering is not induced from the target dataset's expression data; it relies solely on external pretrained embeddings (GeneCompass) and PPI priors, which may limit its ability to capture context-specific programs. The claim 'induces gene programs from data' is somewhat misleading.

The balanced cluster size constraint is a strong assumption that may not reflect biological reality; its justification as an architectural regularizer is reasonable but could confound biological interpretation of the modules.

The supervised biological losses (cluster correlation alignment and pathway-informed optimal transport) use ground truth perturbation-specific statistics during training, which may lead to overfitting to training perturbations and potentially inflate performance on biological metrics; holdout results mitigate this concern but do not eliminate it.

Missing comparison with recent relevant methods such as scDFM (Yu et al., 2026), which is cited for dataset partitioning but not evaluated as a baseline, despite being a direct competitor in flow-matching-based perturbation prediction.

Minor presentation issues: inconsistent metric names in tables (e.g., ρΔ0 vs ρΔD, ACCΔ0 vs ACCΔD), typographical errors in table type labels (e.g., 'Sca', 'Gpa', 'Sina', 'Oda'), and the claim of 'surpasses 13 leading methods' includes trivial baselines (Control, Linear).

The reported average improvement of 6.7% over the strongest baselines is not clearly defined or easily verifiable from the tables; some metrics show much larger gains, while others (e.g., on ComboSciPlex) show modest gains.
The attention shift analysis is anecdotal (two case studies) and does not constitute rigorous mechanistic validation.

strengths: Broad and multi-faceted evaluation: three datasets (Norman additive/holdout, Replogle RPE1, ComboSciPlex), 13 baselines, many point-wise/directional/distributional metrics, paired Wilcoxon tests (Table 14), and 5-seed standard deviations (Tables 11–12). This is more thorough than typical perturbation-prediction papers.

The biological motivation for a module-level inductive bias is coherent and reasonable, and the ablation suite (Tables 6a–6e, Fig. 5–6) attempts to isolate the contributions of GRC, GCAE, PPI priors, GeneCompass embeddings, and the two alignment losses.

Reproducibility artifacts are present: detailed hyperparameters (Table 16), full algorithms (Algorithms 1–3), explicit metric definitions (Eqs. 10–18), dataset split statistics (Table 17), and a training-time efficiency analysis (Tables 7–9).

The limitations section (A.8) is honest, explicitly acknowledging that induced modules are a static approximation, that performance is sensitive to the quality/coverage of external priors, and that evaluation scope is limited to two Perturb-seq benchmarks.
weaknesses: Central methodological ambiguity regarding the structure-aware alignment targets. The Cluster Correlation target R*_gt(p) and Pathway OT target S*_gt are per-perturbation statistics derived from ground-truth perturbed cells (Algorithm 3, lines 4–6). The paper never clarifies how these targets are obtained at inference for unseen/combinatorial perturbations. If they are used at test time this is a form of transductive/label leakage that would invalidate the unseen-perturbation claims; if they are training-only, the paper must state so. As written, the mechanism that differentiates scBIG is not reproducible from the text.

Baseline fairness is questionable. CellOracle is run with n_iters reduced from 100,000 to 1,000, yielding a near-zero ρΔ = 0.0437 (Table 1) that is implausibly poor and is not a credible comparison. Foundation models (scGPT, scFoundation, GeneCompass, CellFM) are adapted via the GEARS pipeline for only ~20 epochs and consistently underperform even the Linear baseline; the paper's own ablation (Table 6e) shows that GeneCompass embeddings can degrade conditioning, suggesting the foundation-model baselines may be under-tuned, which would inflate scBIG's relative gains.

Selective reporting of the headline gain. The abstract's '6.7% average improvement over the strongest baselines' is computed against a different 'strongest' baseline per metric (e.g., CellFlow on ρΔ, GeneCompass on PDS), which overstates a consistent advantage and does not reflect a single fair reference point.

Limited novelty relative to the claim of being 'among the first to formalize a module-level inductive bias.' OT-based gene clustering, Perceiver-style latent bottlenecks, conditional flow matching, and OT/correlation alignment losses are all off-the-shelf; the contribution is essentially their combination, and the paper does not compare against prior module/cluster-based perturbation methods in a controlled way.

Presentation and correctness issues that undermine confidence: garbled 'Type' labels in the main tables ('Sca', 'Gpa', 'Sina', 'Ola', 'Ours'), inconsistent publication years in the 'Public' column (e.g., GEARS labeled '23' though the reference is 2024), a truncated code URL, and a suspiciously uniform 'win on every metric' pattern with some very large margins (e.g., PDS 0.7440 vs Control 0.5000 in the holdout double setting) that are not explained.

The balanced-cluster constraint (|c_k| = G/K) is acknowledged to be an architectural regularizer rather than a biological property, but the consequences for interpreting the 'modules' and for the enrichment/attention analyses in §3.5 are not examined; the mechanistic claims (e.g., NOL8 → mTORC1 attention shift) are post hoc and not validated against controls.

Several key components depend on external resources (STRING PPI threshold, Reactome pathway membership, GeneCompass embeddings) whose coverage and context-mismatch are acknowledged in A.8 but not quantified, so it is unclear how much of the reported gain is attributable to the architecture versus the specific priors.

strengths: Clear, biologically grounded motivation: the paper makes a coherent case that perturbation responses are program-level rather than gene-independent, and translates this into a concrete three-stage design (module induction, structured generative modeling, structure-aware alignment).

Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: three datasets (Norman additive/holdout, Replogle2022_rpe1, ComboSciPlex drug perturbation), 13 baselines spanning statistical, foundation, graph-based, and generative paradigms, plus distribution-level metrics and paired Wilcoxon significance tests. The consistent SOTA across most metrics supports the central claim.

Well-designed ablations that isolate the contribution of individual components (GRC vs K-means vs no clustering; GCAE vs standard Transformer; each biological loss; PPI vs GeneCompass priors; loss weights; pooling strategies), which directly supports the 'module-inductive' claim rather than just asserting it.

Strong reproducibility: code release, explicit hyperparameters (Table 16), full algorithmic pseudocode (Algorithms 1–3), multi-seed robustness with reported standard deviations, and confidence intervals for the clustering/encoder comparison.

Biological interpretability beyond black-box prediction: post-hoc Reactome enrichment of GRC modules, perturbation-specific cross-module coordination with bootstrap stability, and differential-attention case studies (NOL8→mTORC1, KCTD10→G2/M) provide evidence that the induced modules are functionally meaningful.

Honest treatment of limitations and ethics: the limitations section candidly discusses static/approximate module structure, prior-dependence, and limited evaluation scope, and the impact statement is appropriately cautious about clinical use.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is largely combinatorial: OT-based balanced clustering, Perceiver-style bottleneck attention, conditional flow matching, and OT/correlation alignment losses are all established components. The 'module-level inductive bias' is a reasonable framing but not a fundamentally new mechanism, so originality is moderate.

Potential confound in the headline comparison: scBIG operates on a learned, pretrained encoder–decoder latent space while CellFlow (its strongest baseline) uses PCA latents. Part of the reported gain may reflect representational capacity rather than module induction per se; the ablations partially address this but do not fully disentangle the two effects.

Several improvements are marginal and the '6.7% average' headline is driven by a subset of metrics (e.g., Norman additive ACCΔ 0.9197 vs 0.9151; drug MSE 0.0451 vs 0.0461). Reporting a single averaged number can overstate the breadth of the advantage.

Reuse of the Reactome knowledge base: it is used both in the pathway-informed OT training loss and as the external audit for cluster enrichment. Although GRC induction itself does not use Reactome, the validation is not fully independent of a resource the model is optimized against, which weakens the 'external' audit claim.

The equal-sized cluster constraint (|c_k| = G/K) is biologically implausible; the paper acknowledges this and frames it as an architectural regularizer, but the downstream consequences (e.g., forcing large programs to be split or merging unrelated genes) are not empirically probed.

Presentation issues: figure/table rendering artifacts and dense tables make some results hard to parse, and a few claims (e.g., 'among the first') are slightly overreaching relative to the incremental nature of the contribution.
